'''Janet Rideout''' is an American [[Organic chemistry|organic chemist]] and one of the scientists who discovered that [[Zidovudine|azidothymidine]] (AZT) could be used as an antiretroviral agent to treat [[HIV|Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)]].<ref name=":12" /> She also played a key role in the development of [[Aciclovir|acyclovir]], the first effective treatment for [[herpes simplex virus]].<ref name=":7" />

== Early life and education ==
Janet Rideout was born Janet Litster January 6, 1939, in Bennington, Vermont. She received bachelor's and master's degrees in chemistry from [[Mount Holyoke College]].<ref name=":12" /> She then earned a PhD in organic chemistry from  [[State University of New York Buffalo|State University of New York, Buffalo]] in 1968.<ref name=":4" />

== Research and career ==
Shortly before graduation from the [[State University of New York Buffalo|State University of New York, Buffalo]], Rideout was hired by chemist and future [[Nobel Prize|Nobel]] laureate [[Gertrude B. Elion|Gertrude Elion]] to work at a small US subsidiary of the British pharmaceutical company [[GlaxoSmithKline|Burroughs Wellcome Company]] (now GlaxoSmithKline).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=D.|first=Grover, N.|date=2011-11-15|title=Contribution of Women Scientists to Pharmacology: A Historical Perspective|url=http://ijpt.iums.ac.ir/browse.php?a_code=A-10-100-234&slc_lang=en&sid=1&sw=Contribution+of+Women+Scientists|journal=Iranian Journal of Pharmacology and Therapeutics|language=en|volume=10|issue=2}}</ref> Initially located in [[Tuckahoe (village), New York]], the branch moved to [[Research Triangle|Research Triangle, North Carolina]], in 1970.<ref name=":2"/>

Rideout specialized in [[nucleoside]] chemistry. Nucelosides are chemical compounds consisting of a [[pentose]] sugar bound to a [[nitrogenous base]]. When [[Phosphorylation|phosphorylated]], nucleosides become [[nucleotide]]s, which are the building blocks of [[nucleic acid]]s ([[DNA]] and [[RNA]]).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lodish|first1=Harvey|last2=Berk|first2=Arnold|last3=Zipursky|first3=S. Lawrence|last4=Matsudaira|first4=Paul|last5=Baltimore|first5=David|last6=Darnell|first6=James|date=2000|title=Structure of Nucleic Acids|url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21514/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190924224956/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK21514/|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 24, 2019|journal=Molecular Cell Biology. 4th Edition|language=en}}</ref> As such, they're needed for replication (copying of the genome before cells divide so that each gets a copy). Therefore, cells that replicate frequently, such as cancer cells and bacteria have a high demand for nucleosides. Recognizing this, teams of scientists, including a team at Burroughs Wellcome including Janet Rideout dedicated themselves to studying [[Structural analog|chemical analogs]] that could mimic natural nucleosides, inhibiting replication.<ref name=":6" />

=== Arabinosides ===
One branch of Rideout's research involved the synthesis of [[purine]] [[Arabinose|arabinosides]] (similar in structure to the canonical [[nucleoside]]s found in DNA and RNA, but containing the sugar [[arabinose]] instead of [[ribose]] or [[deoxyribose]]). Rideout synthesized the nucleoside analog diaminopurine arabinoside, which was found to be active against [[herpes simplex virus]] and [[Vaccinia|vaccinia virus]] and with a lower toxicity than similar compounds.<ref name=":2"/> In her Nobel lecture, [[Gertrude B. Elion|Gertrude Elion]] credits this finding with initiating her group's "antiviral odyssey," which would lead to the development of the [[HIV]] treatment [[Zidovudine|AZT]], the [[Herpes simplex|herpes]] treatment [[Aciclovir|acyclovir]], and other important [[antiretroviral]] compounds.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Elion|first=G. B.|date=1989-04-07|title=The purine path to chemotherapy|journal=Science|language=en|volume=244|issue=4900|pages=41–47|doi=10.1126/science.2649979|issn=0036-8075|pmid=2649979|bibcode=1989Sci...244...41E}}</ref>

The promising results from diaminopurine arabinoside led Rideout to synthesize additional purine arabinosides, in hopes of developing more effective [[Antiviral drug|antivirals]]. She worked with a team including virologists J. Bauer and P. Collins to study their pharmacological properties, discovering that aminopurine arabinosides had antiviral activity that was dependent on their amino group.<ref name=":7" /> This knowledge helped lead to the design of more potent antiviral medications including [[Aciclovir|acyclovir]], the first active selective drug against [[Herpes simplex|herpes]] viruses.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iDNy0XxGqT8C&q=janet+rideout+++chemist&pg=PA380|title=The Evolution of Drug Discovery: From Traditional Medicines to Modern Drugs|last=Ravina|first=Enrique|date=2011-01-11|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9783527326693|language=en}}</ref>

=== AZT ===
Rideout also studied nucleosides' antibacterial properties. One of the compounds that interested her was azidothymidine (AZT), identical to the canonical nucleoside thymidine found in DNA except for the 3' position, where AZT has an azide (N3) group instead of a hydroxyl (OH) group. That 3' OH is needed for linking nucleotides together, so AZT could potentially act as a chain terminator (it could be added to a growing nucleic acid chain, but additional nucleotides couldn't link to it).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sites.tufts.edu/hivprevention/nrtis/|title=NRTIs {{!}} HIV treatment and prevention|website=sites.tufts.edu|access-date=2018-09-19}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

AZT was first synthesized in 1964 by a Michigan Cancer Foundation researcher, [[Jerome Horwitz]], with hopes it could be used to treat [[leukemia]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=A Master of Science History {{!}} SpringerLink|volume=30|language=en-gb|doi=10.1007/978-94-007-2627-7|series=Archimedes|year=2012|isbn=978-94-007-2626-0|last1=Buchwald|first1=Jed Z.}}</ref> but it wasn't found to be effective and raised toxicity concerns so it was abandoned.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1990/11/05/74308/index.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080502191421/http://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1990/11/05/74308/index.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 2, 2008|title=THE INSIDE STORY OF THE AIDS DRUG For the first time Burroughs Wellcome tells how it made crucial decisions on AZT that brought howls from Congress and gay groups. Some of its wounds were self-inflicted. - November 5, 1990|website=archive.fortune.com|access-date=2018-09-16}}</ref> There was  limited research on it in the following years, including a report from a laboratory in showing it had activity against [[Friend virus]], a murine virus that causes leukemia in mice,<ref name=":6" /> but retroviruses weren't thought to affect humans, and the paper drew little attention.<ref name=":8" />

Rideout was interested in AZT's other potential applications; she studied AZT as an antibacterial agent at the Burroughs Wellcome Company for several years.<ref>{{cite book|author=Nathalia Holt|title=Cured: How the Berlin Patients Defeated HIV and Forever Changed Medical Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IG3aBYLDgaUC&pg=PT40|date=2014-02-27|publisher=Penguin Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-698-14854-3|pages=40–}}</ref> The compound was particularly effective against [[gram-negative bacteria]].<ref name=":5">{{Citation|title=Therapeutic nucleosides|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/CA1302263C/en|department =(issue-date 1986-09-16)|access-date=2018-09-19}}</ref> In addition to chemical characterization and optimization of its synthesis, their research included pharmacokinetic and safety testing in rats.<ref name=":9" /> This experience, and the data they collected showing that the drug was tolerated in rats placed them in a prime position to expedite the drug development process.<ref name=":2"/><ref name=":9" />

In June 1984, Burroughs Wellcome initiated a program to identify chemical compounds that might be effective against HIV, and they put Rideout in charge of choosing which compounds to test.<ref name=":2"/> There was limited knowledge about HIV at the time, but Rideout's search was aided by the finding that HIV was a [[retrovirus]], a type of virus that transfers between cells with its genome encoded in RNA but, once it infects a host cell, reverse transcribes its RNA genome into a DNA copy which it then inserts into the host cell's DNA, so that the cell and all its progeny are perpetually infected. Knowing that HIV was a retrovirus, Rideout searched for compounds with antiretroviral activity; the company didn't have the necessary set-up for studying live HIV, so they screened against animal retroviruses,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://casetext.com/case/burroughs-wellcome-v-barr-laboratories|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920050012/https://casetext.com/case/burroughs-wellcome-v-barr-laboratories|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 20, 2018|title=BURROUGHS WELLCOME v. BARR LABORATORIES, 828 F. Supp. 1208 {{!}} Casetext|website=casetext.com|language=en|access-date=2018-09-16}}</ref> with the screening carried out by virologist Martha (Marty) St. Clair.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news|url=https://www.rdmag.com/article/2007/09/quarter-century-battling-hivaids|title=A Quarter Century of Battling HIV/AIDS|date=2007-09-06|work=Research & Development|access-date=2018-09-16|language=en}}</ref>

One of the compounds Rideout chose to test was AZT and by the end of 1984, Wellcome had shown that AZT was active against two animal retroviruses, Harvey sarcoma virus and Friend leukemia virus.<ref name=":2" /> To see if it was also active against HIV, they collaborated with scientists at the [[National Cancer Institute]] (NCI), including [[Samuel Broder]] and [[Hiroaki Mitsuya|Hiroaka Mitsuya]], who had developed a method to grow the virus in immortalized human [[T helper cell|T4 cells]] (the type of immune cell HIV targets).<ref name=":9">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cb6BOkj9fK4C&q=janet+rideout+++14+compounds&pg=PA261|title=Drug Discovery: A History|last=Sneader|first=Walter|date=2005-06-23|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9780471899792|language=en}}</ref> NCI found AZT to be highly effective against HIV in these cells,<ref name=":2" /> and it went on to become the first FDA-approved treatment for HIV.

In 1985, Rideout, along with four other BW scientists, applied for American and British patents for the use of AZT, given the chemical name zidovudine and the proprietary name Retrovir, for the treatment of HIV-1; they were approved in 1988, with Rideout is listed as the first co-inventor.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|url=http://www.alanrwalker.com/assets/PDF/HIV-Retrovir-v3.pdf|title=Contrary life and technical fixes : from malaria vaccine to hormone contraceptive|last=R.)|first=Walker, Alan (Alan|year=2015|isbn=9780954517328|location=Edinburgh|oclc=936629901|access-date=2018-09-19|archive-date=2018-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920083859/http://www.alanrwalker.com/assets/PDF/HIV-Retrovir-v3.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Rideout's research on AZT didn't stop with its initial application to HIV. In the coming years at Burroughs Wellcome, she helped elucidate how AZT is processed in the body (administered as the cell membrane-permeable [[nucleoside]], it is [[Phosphorylation|phosphorylated]] inside cells to the [[nucleotide]] form which is used in DNA synthesis) and how it selectively targets HIV's [[reverse transcriptase]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=Furman|first1=P. A.|last2=Fyfe|first2=J. A.|last3=Clair|first3=M. H. St|last4=Weinhold|first4=K.|last5=Rideout|first5=J. L.|last6=Freeman|first6=G. A.|last7=Lehrman|first7=S. N.|last8=Bolognesi|first8=D. P.|last9=Broder|first9=S.|date=1986-11-01|title=Phosphorylation of 3'-azido-3'-deoxythymidine and selective interaction of the 5'-triphosphate with human immunodeficiency virus reverse transcriptase|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=83|issue=21|pages=8333–8337|doi=10.1073/pnas.83.21.8333|issn=0027-8424|pmid=2430286|pmc=386922|bibcode=1986PNAS...83.8333F|doi-access=free}}</ref> She also continued to look into AZT's other potential uses, including against other viruses and bacteria.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|last1=Elwell|first1=L. P.|last2=Ferone|first2=R.|last3=Freeman|first3=G. A.|last4=Fyfe|first4=J. A.|last5=Hill|first5=J. A.|last6=Ray|first6=P. H.|last7=Richards|first7=C. A.|last8=Singer|first8=S. C.|last9=Knick|first9=V. B.|date=1987-02-01|title=Antibacterial activity and mechanism of action of 3'-azido-3'-deoxythymidine (BW A509U).|journal=Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy|language=en|volume=31|issue=2|pages=274–280|doi=10.1128/AAC.31.2.274|issn=0066-4804|pmid=3551832|pmc=174705}}</ref>

=== Later career ===
In 1995, after working at Burroughs Wellcome for over 26 years, and rising to the rank of associate division director, Rideout joined Inspire Pharmaceuticals (acquired by [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] in 2011)<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-merck-inspire/merck-to-acquire-inspire-pharma-for-430-million-idUSTRE7345EA20110405|title=Merck to acquire Inspire Pharma for $430 million|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=2018-09-19|language=en-US}}</ref> as Director of Chemistry.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasdaq.com/markets/ipos/filing.ashx?filingid=451752|title=INSPIRE PHARMACEUTICALS INC (Form: S-1/A, Received: 03/30/2000 08:14:21)|website=www.nasdaq.com|access-date=2018-09-18}}</ref> She subsequently had a number of promotions within the company: to Senior Director of Discovery in June 1996, Vice President in January 1998, and Senior Vice President of Discovery in February 2000.<ref name=":4" />

At Inspire Pharmaceuticals, she continued researching nucelosides but now as activators ([[agonist]]s) instead of inhibitors. In addition to their role in the biosynthesis of [[nucleic acid]]s, nucleotides can serve as important signaling molecules including through activating [[purinergic receptor]]s. Rideout helped develop ways to synthesize a type of purinergic receptor agonist called dinucleoside polyphosphates (dinucleotides), which consist of two joined nucleosides with varying numbers of phosphate groups, so they can be further studied.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shaver|first1=Sammy R.|last2=Rideout|first2=Janet L.|last3=Pendergast|first3=William|last4=Douglass|first4=James G.|last5=Brown|first5=Edward G.|last6=Boyer|first6=José L.|last7=Patel|first7=Roshni I.|last8=Redick|first8=Catherine C.|last9=Jones|first9=Arthur C.|date=2005-03-07|title=Structure–activity relationships of dinucleotides: Potent and selective agonists of P2Y receptors|journal=Purinergic Signalling|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=183–191|doi=10.1007/s11302-005-0648-2|issn=1573-9546|pmc=2096529|pmid=18404503}}</ref>

Rideout retired in September 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://people.equilar.com/bio/janet-rideout-inspire-pharmaceuticals/salary/34308|title=Janet J. Rideout Ph.D. - Executive Bio, Work History, and Contacts - Equilar BoardEdge|website=people.equilar.com|access-date=2018-09-19|archive-date=2018-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920045919/http://people.equilar.com/bio/janet-rideout-inspire-pharmaceuticals/salary/34308|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Rideout holds over 40 U.S. patents.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Maynard|first=Lauren Newkirk|date=Summer 2014|title=A Pioneer in the Fight Against AIDS|url=http://www.buffalo.edu/atbuffalo/past-issues/summer-2014/article-page-summer-2014.host.html/content/shared/www/atbuffalo/articles/summer-2014/alumni-life/a-pioneer-in-the-fight-against-aids.detail.html|journal=AtBuffalo|volume=Summer 2014}}</ref> In addition to the patent for treating HIV with AZT, she holds patents for synthesis procedures of various nucleoside analogs as well as their specific therapeutic applications; this includes derivatives of AZT for use treating and preventing infection by certain [[retrovirus]]es and [[gram-negative bacteria]].<ref name=":5" />

== Honors and awards ==

* Distinguished Chemist award, North Carolina Institute of Chemists, 1994<ref name=":4" />
* Dean's Award, [[University at Buffalo|State University of New York, Buffalo]], College of Arts and Science, 2012<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://arts-sciences.buffalo.edu/alumni/alumni-awards.html|title=Alumni Awards - College of Arts and Sciences - University at Buffalo|website=arts-sciences.buffalo.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-19|archive-date=2018-09-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920045909/http://arts-sciences.buffalo.edu/alumni/alumni-awards.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* [[University at Buffalo|State University of New York, Buffalo]] Alumni Association, Distinguished Alumni Award, March 2014<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=http://www.buffalo.edu/news/releases/2014/03/026.html|title=13 to be honored by the UB Alumni Association - University at Buffalo|website=www.buffalo.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-16}}</ref>
* Life fellow and member of board of directors, [[American Institute of Chemists]]<ref name=":4" />
